body.text: In short:
The government has backed down on planned changes to working holiday visas.
The cap on third-year visas will rise from 5,000 to 25,000, while second-year applicants will have tougher regional work requirements.
What's next?
British backpackers remain exempt from regional work rules.

The government has backed down on its planned overhaul of the working holiday-maker program, agreeing to increase the number of backpackers eligible for a third-year visa and tightening regional work requirements.
Under changes announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, working holiday-makers would need to complete 120 days of regional work, up from 88 days, to qualify for a second-year visa.
In a major speech in September, Mr Burke had announced third-year visas would be capped at 5,000 places, a reduction on the current level of about 31,000.

That cap will now be set at 25,000 places, while the introduction of a ballot system called the Next Year Regional Work Guarantee has also been delayed to next year after it was originally scheduled to start in November.

The shift follows months of pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors over the government's original proposal, with businesses warning it would significantly reduce the supply of seasonal workers and leave them struggling to fill jobs over summer.

The new arrangements will apply from March 1, while backpackers who complete their regional work requirements before that date will remain eligible under the existing rules, creating a transition period for those already in the country.
The cap on second-year places would be set at 45,000.

Mr Burke rejected suggestions the government was abandoning its original reforms, arguing the final package had been shaped by consultations with industry and would ultimately deliver more workers to regional Australia.

"From the day after the speech … we started consultation with industry to work through what is the best landing place to deliver the total numbers that we're talking about, but to do it in a way that works best for industry," he said.
"This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them."

He said the government had been able to refine its approach because of a go-slow in visa processing which had created "head room" to adjust the broader working holiday-maker reforms while still pursuing an overall lower migration number.
The number of backpackers getting visas to Australia has fallen dramatically since July, when the go-slow was introduced as a temporary fix designed to put the brakes on international arrivals.

Since then, 44,469 visas have been approved, which means a total of 177,876 backpackers would be granted entry to Australia this financial year, if the government maintains its current rate of processing.
Last financial year, a record 323,077 backpacker visas were granted in Australia.
Mr Burke said Australia would continue to welcome working holiday-makers.
"These reforms make the program fairer, more targeted and sustainable for the long term," he said.
Opposition rubbishes changes as 'complete nonsense'
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described the proposal as "complete nonsense" and vowed to repeal the changes if the Coalition was elected.
"They've created a complete mess with this raffle, this ballot. They've said they're going to delay it … they should just axe it," he said.
The sentiment was echoed by Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said the backdown was "inevitable" but warned the government had already damaged confidence in the sector.
The National Farmers' Federation welcomed the changes but said key questions remained unanswered.
"We need more details on the logistical realities of this reform before we can fully throw our support behind it," president Hamish McIntyre said.
In WA, Premier Roger Cook acknowledged the federal government's need to bring down net overseas migration, but said he would make sure it "doesn't impact on Western Australia's economy".
He said he hoped further adjustment to the system would improve the number of working holiday-makers heading west.
"What I want to see is less people going to the east coast and more people coming to the west coast," Mr Cook said.
British backpackers the elephant in the room
None of the changes to the proposal would affect British backpackers, who remain exempt from regional work rules under the Australia–UK free trade agreement.

The favourable treatment has helped drive a sharp increase in British backpacker numbers, from 47,238 in 2023–24 to 79,412 in 2024–25, complicating the government's efforts to reduce migration while maintaining regional workforces.

Last week, Mr Burke insisted overall cuts to backpackers must remain unchanged, a reduction of about 40,000 a year, while acknowledging Australia must "find a way" to reduce the amount of working holiday-makers coming from the UK within the boundaries of the free trade agreement.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had previously ruled out imposing regional work requirements on backpackers from the UK, which apply to other working holiday-makers seeking to extend their visas beyond 12 months.

But earlier this month, he hinted at a rethink ahead of meetings with his British counterpart in the Caribbean, saying backpackers should experience more than just Bondi and Coogee — a nod to possible regional work requirements.

"What we're after is putting forward the benefits that backpackers who travel to Australia have in having the full Australian experience, not just experiencing Coogee and Bondi, but also experiencing the wonders of regional Australia, and so that can be a major benefit for them as well as for Australia," Mr Albanese said.

It is unclear whether the government would have to negotiate a wholesale rewrite of the backpacker element of the free trade agreement, or if it could be changed by regulation agreed to by the UK government.
Mr Burke said the government was wary of "retaliation" but said he was confident the UK government had a "good understanding" of the issues that need to be resolved.
"I'm not going to put a timeline on it, but I will say I'm very optimistic about how those conversations have been going," he said.
"We've got constructive conversations that are continuing with the United Kingdom, and I'm optimistic that we're going to get a much better deal than what was previously negotiated."
